summary:
Curiosity Traverse Explorer is an interactive map designed to bring NASA’s Curiosity rover journey across Gale Crater to life. It combines an interactive map with an immersive first-person view of every recorded stop, allowing users to explore the Martian terrain while comparing it with the actual images captured by the rover.

The platform brings together 42,317 rover positions and 10,327 science targets, layered over HiRISE imagery from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. Using the USGS 1-meter elevation model, users can explore a 3D version of the Martian landscape, virtually walk across the surface, retrace the rover’s journey, or view the terrain from above.

The first-person experience places users at a human eye level of 1.7 meters, with options to switch to the rover’s camera height or a drone-like view at 15 meters. Each stop includes coordinates, elevation, slope, geological information, and rover images, organized by sol and scientific target.

This project matters because future Mars exploration depends on understanding the terrain before traveling across it. Knowing the distance, slope, and conditions of a destination is essential for planning a safe route. By clearly showing the limitations of each dataset and cross-checking different sources, our platform helps users understand how reliable the information is and what it means for future journeys on Mars.
details:
We created Curiosity Traverse Explorer to give people a better idea of what it would actually be like to explore Mars. Instead of just looking at maps and numbers, users can explore the same terrain that NASA's Curiosity rover has travelled across. The app brings together information from different NASA missions and USGS datasets to create an interactive view of Gale Crater.

It includes all (currently) 42,317 recorded rover positions and 10,327 science targets, displayed over high-resolution HiRISE imagery. Users can follow Curiosity's journey, measure distances, search for specific locations, and see how the elevation changes along the way.

One of the most interesting features is the first-person view. It lets users experience the Martian landscape from a human perspective, with the ability to look around, walk across the terrain, and replay the rover's drives. Users can also explore actual rover photographs and see information about each location.

What the project does and how it works

The main idea was to bring everything someone might need to explore Curiosity's journey into one application. Rather than having to open several different maps and websites, users can find most of the information they need in one place.

Following Curiosity's journey: The main 2D map shows the rover's route, parking locations, drive positions, and science targets. Users can search by sol, site, drive, or target name. They can also filter by date range and measure distances between different locations.

Walking around Mars: One of the main features is the first-person view, which lets users experience the terrain instead of just looking at it from above. It uses the USGS 1 m elevation model, with a 2 m terrain mesh near the rover's route and an 8 m mesh farther away. Users can look around, walk through the landscape, change their eye height, and replay the rover's journey.

Understanding the terrain: Each location provides information such as elevation, heading, roll, pitch, and geological unit. There is also an elevation profile that shows how the terrain changes as the rover moves along its route, including where it climbs and descends.

Seeing the rover’s scientific targets: Science targets are marked directly on the map, so users can see where Curiosity carried out its research. Geological layers help show the different types of terrain, and actual rover photographs are attached to the locations where they were taken.

How different NASA missions are brought together

A big part of this project was figuring out how to combine information from different sources and make it all work together. We used Curiosity (MSL) rover positions, science targets, and raw images, HiRISE imagery from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, JPL Mars Trek map tiles, USGS elevation models and geological maps, and more.

Claude Code was utilized heavily to combine these sources and datasets, writing the code behind our project. 

Benefits

One of the biggest benefits of the app is convenience. Information that would normally be spread across different tools and websites is now available in one place. Users can move between the rover's route, terrain, photographs, science targets, and geological information without constantly switching between different applications. We wanted the site to be useful without making the information seem more accurate than it really is. Limitations are highlighted in the limitation section of our site. 

Intended impact

The app is intended for people who are interested in Mars, including scientists, students, researchers, and mission planners.

It gives them a way to explore parts of Mars without needing access to an actual rover or complicated scientific software. They can follow Curiosity's route, get a better sense of the landscape, look at elevation changes, and see the photographs taken along the way.

It could also be useful when thinking about future exploration. Understanding how steep a route is, what the terrain looks like, and what is located nearby can all help when considering where a rover might travel next.

More broadly, the project shows how information from different NASA missions and publicly available scientific resources can be brought together to create something interactive and easy to use, without ignoring the problems or limitations that come with the data.

Tools and technologies

A combination of different technologies was used to build the application. Claude Code was utilized heavily to synthesize and create our final site utilizing the tools below. 

  • React and TypeScript: Used to build the frontend and handle the main application.
  • Vite: Used for development and building the application.
  • Three.js: Powers the 3D terrain and first-person exploration experience.
  • Vitest: Used to test different parts of the application.
  • Python and FastAPI: Used for the backend.
  • Vercel: Used to host the application.

The project also relies on several scientific datasets and services, including:

  • MSL Analyst's Notebook.
  • NASA MMGIS.
  • PDS PLACES.
  • USGS MSL Gale elevation model and geological map.
  • HiRISE imagery.
  • Mars Trek.
  • NASA's raw-image service.

The entire project was coded on the VS Code platform, with significant assistance from Claude Code.

Creativity and innovation

What makes this project interesting is that it takes information that would normally just be numbers, coordinates, and map data and turns it into something people can actually interact with.

The first-person mode is a good example of this. Instead of simply showing where Curiosity has travelled, it lets users step into a recreation of the Martian landscape and explore it from ground level. This makes it much easier to imagine what the rover's surroundings might actually look like.

Another feature we wanted to include was the ability to see real rover photographs at the locations where they were taken. This helps connect the map to the actual exploration and gives users a better understanding of what Curiosity encountered along its journey.

Factors considered during development

There were a few challenges that had to be considered while building the site. Some were related to the data itself, while others came down to making sure the experience was smooth and practical to use. Our major factors are listed below.

  • Position accuracy: The PLACES and Analyst's Notebook datasets don't always agree on rover positions. To avoid mixing inconsistent coordinates, the site uses the Notebook positions as its main reference.
  • Missing information: There are gaps in the available rover data. For sols 4844–5073, only end-of-drive waypoints are available, so the app cannot show every intermediate position.
  • Performance: Showing detailed 3D terrain over a large area can become demanding. To keep things running smoothly, the highest terrain detail is limited to approximately 35 m around the rover's route, with less detailed terrain farther away.
  • Data reliability: The geological map is useful for understanding the broader area, but it isn't detailed enough to represent exact ground-level conditions. The app makes this clear so users don't mistake regional information for precise local measurements.
